from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('pages:', len(r.pages))
print('metadata:', r.metadata)
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 text=p.extract_text()
 parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+text)
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:2]))
PY"

p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for i in range(1,18):
 for suffix in ('txt','png'):
  (p / f'page-{i:02d}.{suffix}').unlink(missing_ok=True)
(p / 'manuscript.txt').unlink(missing_ok=True)
print('Removed temporary extraction and rendering files; manuscript unchanged.')
PY"

strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent training method: shared-weight predictions on masked inputs learn from detached predictions on full inputs alongside ordinary supervised learning. It adds no inference overhead, and token removal reduces the additional training cost for ViTs.

The central improvements over strong training recipes are well supported. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across ViT sizes and training lengths. Three-run results in Table A.12 strengthen this evidence: ViT-B improves from 83.46 ± 0.04 to 84.08 ± 0.02.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional computation. Table 7 shows ViT-B reaching 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for longer baseline training in 26 GPU-days. Comparisons with CoSub and GradAug further support the method's practical accuracy–cost tradeoff.

Evaluation is broad, covering ResNet, Swin, several pretrained-model fine-tuning recipes, transfer learning, and dense prediction. Tables A.2–A.4 demonstrate benefits beyond ImageNet classification, including 0.4–0.6 mIoU gains on ADE20K and an ImageNet-A improvement from 51.9% to 58.3% for ViT-H.

The distillation, masking-ratio, and loss-weight ablations provide useful supporting evidence. The equations, concise pseudocode, detailed recipe tables, and supplied code link make the principal method reasonably reproducible. Together, the repeatable improvements and practical simplicity support weak acceptance.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental relative to existing self-distillation, asymmetric-view training, and submodel regularization. The strongest contribution is their effective integration with token masking. Also, Table 6 compares methods using different training recipes; lower historical accuracies do not establish that earlier self-distillation methods are incompatible with RSB, as the text asserts.

The proposed mechanism is overstated. Section 3.1 claims masking effectively applies exclusively to successfully predicted images, but Equation 3 distills every sample, including confidently incorrect predictions. Figure 3's aggregate gradient norms support an evolving training signal without establishing correctness-based prioritization. Table A.7 also shows a 1.0-point improvement with zero masking, indicating substantial benefits can arise without masking.

Benefits depend on the task and checkpoint policy. In Table 10, adding MaskSub during ViT-B fine-tuning reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.9% to 89.6%. Section 4.2 explicitly reports unchanged best-checkpoint CLIP accuracy despite improved final-epoch accuracy. These disclosed exceptions constrain the broad claims of consistently significant improvements.

Statistical support is uneven. Although repeated runs substantiate important core results, the 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and small COCO gains lack uncertainty estimates. Some transfer improvements are smaller than the reported variability, such as ViT-S Flowers performance with MaskSub pretraining alone. Confidence in these smaller effects is consequently lower.

There are correctable reporting errors: Table 10 labels the ViT-S Cars change from 80.9% to 92.2% as +1.3 rather than +11.3 points. Section 4.4 claims one-sixth of GradAug's training cost, whereas Table 9 reports 8.6 versus 23.4 GPU-days, approximately 37% of the total cost. These are reporting refinements rather than failures of the central method.
